utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The accused has informed me that he's not getting the translation, so could somebody please take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. You'd better check the channel that he's got on his system, would you? Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. You can now hear, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I understand now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, before this witness should be heard, he had an additional request for protective measures. He informed me that he would now also request voice distortion, and the reason why he has this additional request is, first of all, he thinks that his voice is easy to recognise because he has a very particular melody and way of speaking. And the interpreter, actually, who was with me when we talked about it confirmed that he has a very special voice, easy to recognise. But that is only one point. The more important point is that -- I would now have to go into particulars of the witness and, therefore, I would request private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, would you please stand up and make the declaration. We need the microphone. We need the voice distortion microphone turned on. Thanks. Have the interpreters got the right channel? We had a problem last week. Try again, please, sir. Sorry. Yes. Would you start again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir. I suspect that he's unable to hear me. Would you just check his earphones, please. Can you hear me now? Can you hear me now, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to have the witness shown a sheet of paper which should be in front of everybody in the courtroom by now. Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you couldn't hear what was said when you were sitting here already. Your requests for voice alteration, image alteration, and pseudonym were granted, and we have to avoid to say your name. When you look at the sheet in front of you, there is the name under Witness 111. Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the date below your name, is that your birthday?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, below your birthday, there are a couple of other names. In case you have to mention these names --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- would you please, then, only mention the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That document will be Exhibit P403 --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: It's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: In the village of Mirjanovici, close to Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Bosniak, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many children?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: In the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your profession before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I was a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political party before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the SDA. But I was only a member, not in the leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a particular function, or did you appear and give speeches in the public?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, no, I never made any public appearances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were the interethnic relations before the war between the groups?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: They were good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they deteriorate at a certain point in time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. After the multiparty elections, unfortunately, they did deteriorate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which way, and why?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: People started -- there started to be divisions amongst the people. Propaganda was having its effect. People became more cautious and suspicious towards one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend any rallies of these parties, the SDA and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Only that main rally of the SDA on August 25th, 1990. But I did not attend any SDS rallies. Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the SDA party stand for? What was the main motto of the rally that you attended?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: The main motto of the SDA, and this can be proved and you can see it from their platform, was that it was for a united and sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, possibly within the former Yugoslavia, without Slovenia perhaps, if such a political agreement was reached, because this was appropriate for Bosnia because it was populated by three peoples, three nationalities. And Bosniaks are in such an environment. And I think this was a good concept if political agreement had been reached on that. That's one thing. The other thing is that in the promotion of the party at that rally, it was stated that we wanted a unified foreign policy, a unified currency, a unified army as important elements of a state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you did not attend SDS rallies. Do you, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. nevertheless, know what their main motto was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No. At the end of September in 1990, when they had their main promotional rally in Foca, I was away in Zagreb, so I can't say what their platform was or any particulars that were stated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you follow -- in the months and two years afterwards, did you follow the policy of the SDS through the media?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, globally I did in order to keep myself informed, without wishing to convey that to somebody else or to have any obligation to do that. It was only for me, for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the SDS politicians say about the other ethnic groups? Do you recall anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. In early April, there was some kind of propaganda on Radio Foca where the SDS leader, Miro Stanic, stated that it was not possible to live with Muslim neighbours anymore, Bosniaks; that it was time to clear up once and for all relations with them; that Serbs could not permit themselves to be woken up by the hodza every morning from the mosque minaret; that there was also a danger of the Serb population or Serb units being circumcised and such things, which had a very negative effect in the further separation and division of the Serbian people from their neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned April. Which year, April, were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Stanic. What position did he have?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: He was the president of the SDS at that time. After Petko Cancar, he took over that duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did politicians from the republic level appear in Foca in that time period?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, especially those who were born in Foca. Among them were Mr. Velibor Ostojic and Mr. Maksimovic and they were often visiting Foca. Occasionally Mrs. Plavsic would visit as well. I think she was, out of the three leading figures, Karadzic, and the third one who died, I can't remember exactly - Koljevic - so she was the one who visited most often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Ostojic. What position did he have in the SDS or in the political ranks?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: At that time, he was the information minister in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on behalf of the SDS. Mr. Maksimovic was the president of the club of the Serbian Democratic Party in the Bosnia and Herzegovina parliament, and, of course, he was also a professor at the university.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any of these people speak about the Muslims, and if so, what did they say?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Velibor Ostojic was present as a guest at the rally that I mentioned earlier and he spoke generally. I can't remember any particulars, but I don't think that he said anything in particular against one side or the other at that time. But Mr. Maksimovic, at a rally in Gorazde, stated that in the previous war the Drina River -- blood flowed in the River Drina and now this time blood will flow down both the rivers Drina and Cehotina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this rally in Gorazde when he said that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: This could have happened at the end of 1990, during the period when the parties were doing promotional work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything that Mr. Kovacic said in relation to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I remember only his statement at a session of the B and H parliament when he stated that in the foreseeable future there is a threat that one of the peoples could disappear from these territories. And I think that he meant the Bosniak people, because he knew that the Bosniak people were not armed. They were not prepared for war. They were defenseless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the war in Foca break out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: The war in Foca broke out on April 6, 1992, when the results of the referendum were published in which the majority of Bosniaks and Croats voted for an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina and when the European Community recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign state. This did not suit the SDS at all, so they started to work on the second option.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "second option"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: The war option, because they had the possibility to arm themselves. They had a large potential from the former Yugoslav army that had come to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They came from Croatia and Slovenia. They were located in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So there was a lot of materiel and also staff potential, and that provided the SDS with the opportunity to arm itself very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the war started, how long did it last?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: In the urban areas it was quite short, and you could also say -- if you take into account that the International Community stated that it recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina on April the 5th, then you could say that the 6th of April is the date of aggression on Foca. And it didn't last very long in Foca, but particularly it was in one part of the town where the Muslim forces, a small group of Muslim forces, were resisting. This was in the area of Donje Polje while in the area of the Foca municipality. Outside of the city there was sporadic fighting more or less. People were already escaping. They were running away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in the fighting at any time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No. I was a doctor by profession, so even if there was such an opportunity at military exercises, I felt that I should really perfect my knowledge and that I should work in my area of specialisation, and I didn't have any interest in learning about weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if houses were destroyed during this short period of fighting in Foca town?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. In this area where there was fighting, a large number of Bosniak and a certain number of Serb houses were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if the house of the accused Krnojelac was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where it was situated within Foca and how it got destroyed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. It was quite close (redacted) (redacted). This was close to a small factory which manufactured wooden furniture. It was called Stolarija. I can't remember the street where it was, but I know well what the house looks like. It was -- the facade was of white brick, and there was a small cafe in front of the house, and it had a sort of bamboo fence. So it was easy to set it on fire by an inflammable bullet or in some other way. It was easy to set it on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it set on fire or did it get destroyed during the fighting? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I don't know any details about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the Muslim houses in the Donje Polje neighbourhood, do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Not only in Donje Polje but in the entire region of the town. Wherever there were any private Bosnian homes, they were set on fire. This was the usual thing to do in order to frighten the local population to flee the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I know that -- well, when I was at the provisional camp in Livade there were a lot of houses burning. I could see it from there. And also later from the KP Dom, from the windows, we could see how houses were burning in the surrounding areas and also on the banks of the Drina. Also, a large number of detainees who came after me talked about how this or that house was set on fire after being looted first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just excuse me a moment. Madam Registrar. You go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the photo Exhibit 18/7290. It's the top photo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have to put it on the ELMO; otherwise, we cannot follow what you say. Can you identify the area?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, I can identify the area. This is Donje Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a close look at this photo. Do you see a mosque, and if so, can you point it out to us?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have to point it out on the ELMO, not on the TV, the monitor.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me. This is a photo of Gornje Polje so you can see the Sahat Kula, the tower, the watchtower. Also, there is a mosque, and you can see the dome. So it wasn't destroyed at that time. So this is not Donje Polje. Foca has two areas. This is Gornje Polje. The upper photo shows Gornje Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness had pointed at this little tower at the left-hand side of the photo, right in the middle, and he pointed at the building with the roof, the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the houses behind the mosque, were they Muslim houses? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. These were exclusively Muslim homes, and this area, this neighbourhood is called Granovski Sokak.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to now show you now the photos 7292 and 7293.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what neighbourhood this is?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: This is Donje Polje. This is the neighbourhood of Donje Polje. There is an elevation above that called Celovine where heavy weapons were deployed from which they were firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Heavy weapons of whom? Which side? You said heavy weapons were deployed. Who deployed the heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: This was taken -- these positions were taken by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this photo, do you see a mosque, and if so, can you point it out to us?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. I see a destroyed mosque without a roof. This is the mosque whose name is Na Musluku.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETSLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is pointing at the square building in the middle of the photo, with no roof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the houses around --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Not the roof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I said, without the roof.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the buildings around the mosque, were they inhabited by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: This was inhabited by Muslims. There were a few Serb houses as well. And these big buildings, they were socially-owned buildings, these yellow buildings here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we have the other photo now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the same neighbourhood, just from a slightly different part?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. It's higher up, and you can see more of this part of Celovine, more of the woods and less of the building, the housing complex, because the photograph is shifted a little from the centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show you now again the photograph 18/7292. But, Your Honours, the original photo is a wide-angle photo, and I have here now the left part of this wide-angle photo. Ms. Manas will show us the original photo, but I would like the witness to point something out. Would you put it on the ELMO so that we can see the left-hand side of the -- the left-hand side. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This neighbourhood, is it close to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. You can see even part of the premises where furniture was sold, the furniture that was manufactured in the KP Dom before the war. And what I am showing you now is the bakery. See? And the rest is the neighbourhood of Donje Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness pointed out the bakery, and that is the white building in the right -- in the left-hand corner, standing more or less alone on the photo.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We will talk about the bakery later on. Thank you. Witness, how many mosques were in Foca before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I think that in the entire urban area there were 11 or 13 mosques. I'm not sure, but it's between 11 and 13. If I were to enumerate all of them, it would take us a long time. However, on the territory of the entire municipality, there were between 26 and 30 altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if any of these mosques remained standing after the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, no. All were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like now to discuss your workplace and your arrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And for this I would like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, it seems only fair that we should do so, but have you got anything you want to say about it? This is where he will be identified by what is going to be said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You can tell that it is in private session when you get "PS" across the badge on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: We were taken to the hill of Prevrac. Until then, our hands had been tied. Veselin Cancar, the commander, caught up with us in the meantime and he said, "Who tied these people's hands?" The soldier who had done it was just behind us. He said to the commander that he had done it because he had such orders. When we arrived at the very hill of Prevrac where the family house of one of the parents of Mr. Cancar was, Veselin Cancar, they untied our hands, but they warned us that if anybody tried to escape, they would shoot us. It was night-time by then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken, to which place?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: From that hill we went down a slope by a stream, and we were brought to a place called Livade. There's barbed wire all around it. It was used by the former JNA before. And then just before the war, a trading company had bought the area and there were warehouses there. We were detained in the central building which belonged to the Territorial Defence, and there were all kinds of pieces of military equipment there except for weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you detained at Livade?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: We were there from the 11th until the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived were there already other detainees there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No. No. That night we were the first detainees. And already early in the morning, a large number of detainees were brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many detainees were there altogether in Livade while you were there? What was the highest number?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, I think it was between 80 to 100 persons in a few hangars, excluding women and children. They were separated in the morning and taken to other hangars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity did these people have?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Most of them were Bosniaks. At that moment, a Croat was detained as well. Is it necessary for me to mention his name too?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: His name is Krunoslav Marinovic, and he was brought in quite beaten up. He was caught in the weekend cottage of his wife. And he had blue bruises all other his face, and we thought that his upper jaw had been fractured as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is the person in Schedule C, number 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is before we get to the KP Dom, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but we want to point out that certain people were targeted from the beginning, right from the beginning throughout, until they disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I can understand that this is part of the attack upon the civilian population, if nothing else, and I'm just curious as to why we have to worry about Schedule C when we're still at Livade, but you'll pick up something later on about him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's only -- I wanted to alert you that this person is particularly targeted right from the first moment until the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of Livade? Which particular -- was there a particular commander?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, Veselin Cancar. He himself said that he was commander, and the soldiers also addressed him as "commander." He was the first commander of the camp, the one up there at Livade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to him while you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were brief contacts. That night he escorted us to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you talk about when you talked to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I cannot remember the details. He was frustrated as to why the Bosniaks had opted for a sovereign Bosna. He was cursing and threatening quite a bit, saying things like, "We'll show you. You want a sovereign Bosnia. We'll show you." So that was this rhetoric, but no questions were asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were the conditions in Livade in relation to food, bedding, and hygienic conditions?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Very poor. There was concrete in one part of the building. They used to have a salt warehouse before. There was a lot of humidity there. Hygienic conditions were poor, and also food was not good, and this was not a good place to stay at either. Conditions were poor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone beaten in Livade, any detainees beaten in Livade themselves?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Some of the prisoners who were captured in town itself and brought to Livade from the 11th or, rather, the 12th in the morning until the 17th, already when they were being arrested, they were beaten up, like the mentioned Krunoslav Marinovic. Then Rasim Mezbur, the photographer, he was beaten up that way too, as well as his father-in-law. And especially I would like to point out the beating up of a boy whom they captured in town and brought to our window. On our window, they put a tarpaulin so one could not see through it, and they tied him to the fence, and they were beating him with ropes. We could hear the blows and we could hear his screams and we could hear the rope piercing the air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone killed at Livade; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I don't know whether he survived these blows. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken next from Livade?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: From Livade, in the evening of the 17th of April, we were taken to -- we were taken in freight vehicles covered with tarpaulin, in several groups. I think all of us that night were transferred. I just want to mention that this camp, Livade, served for a long time after that as a transit or collection centre for people to be then transferred to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the KP Dom, how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I stayed in KP Dom from the April 17th, 1992 until July 5th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in KP Dom, who received you? Were they soldiers or policemen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: It was night, and there were both soldiers and policemen there. So there were both policemen and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you registered when you arrived, registered as detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, not right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever registered, put onto lists or whatever?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. In a couple of days, a guard from Serbia went around and he wrote the names and surnames and the professions of the detainees in a large book. He went to all the rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Into which room were you taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I was taken to Room 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you a floor plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 6/2.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, here I'm indicating that room. It's on the ground floor and it's Room 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would ask in future to have a plan, a floor plan, which is not marked, because this one is clearly marked. Room 11 is marked with an arrow. So in future I would like unmarked floor plans to be used as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, is there some real dispute as to whether this witness was in Room 11 or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. But I don't know what the gist of this is. If the witness is indicating something, then he should indicate it on an exhibit that is not marked. Perhaps if he shows some other room and claims it's Room 11, that could be disputed. I don't know. But if we're asking him to identify where Room 11 is, then it's important that this room is not premarked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is no dispute that I have seen at any stage throughout this hearing as to which room was which. Now, if there is going to be a dispute, you'd better say so now, because you have not raised it with any witness. Now, is there a dispute as to whether or not this is a correct floor plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know if we understood one another properly. There is no dispute that this is the right floor plan; however, if the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If there is no dispute that it is a correct floor plan, is there then a dispute that this witness was in Room 11? Now, you've had his statement and I assume his statement says he was in Room 11. Are you going to dispute it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, in the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you going to dispute that he was in Room 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit me, Your Honour, to explain the point of the objection. So far we do not dispute, nor can we dispute, that he was in Room 11; however, if the witness, in an unmarked floor plan, would show some other room, then there would be a doubt whether he was there or not and then the Defence would know or would be suspicious about whether his claims are true or not. A witness could discredit himself or herself in this sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, this trial is going to proceed on the real issues in the case, the issues which have been raised by the parties. We will be here forever if we are going to require each question by the Prosecution to be a nonleading one. Where there is something not in dispute, the Prosecution is at liberty to lead on it. Now, I would have thought the simple question was: Were you in Room 11? Yes. And we would get on to the next question. Unfortunately, we've got to the map. Until you are able to demonstrate, from the fact that you've got the statements and you've read them, that there is going to be a real issue about any of this, the Prosecution can lead on it; otherwise, we will never, ever get to the end of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason why I put the floor plan in front of the witness is not actually Room 11 but what comes now. I put it in front of him without asking where Room 11 was within the building because I thought it was not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But, please, just lead him to the point where there is going to be -- you understood there to be a dispute, and then we won't have this sort of a problem. But so far as we are concerned, if there is no issue about something, you may lead on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And there's certainly no issue as to the accuracy of this floor plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how long did you stay in Room 11?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I stayed two days and two nights in Room 11. Then I was taken to a cell which was outside Room 11, directly under the stairs which lead to the upper floors. This was a small space, it had an entrance, and it was a space underneath the stairs. That's where I stayed for two days and two nights -- I'm sorry, four days and four nights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point out this little cell on the floor plan?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. That would be here. I don't really read these technical drawings very well. But on the same level, as soon as you come out of Room 11, a couple of steps forward you pass the stairs, and then to the left there was a door leading to that cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was pointing in the area where the staircase is indicated on the floor map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So far as I could see, he was pointing mainly at the room with the initials "XC" on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would think this is "WC."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is it? Well, you have a clearer picture than I do. But that's where he seemed to be pointing to. Now, it may be that or the next room, I don't know, but that's where the pointer was showing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: To clarify the matter, with the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness Exhibit 18, the photos 7481 and 7482. According to the index, it's the staircase in this particular area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at the upper photo and also the photo below. Can you explain what you see?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: These photographs show the area from Room 11, in the basement where I was, and number 12 on the right. They also show the staircase to the upper floors, and also the railing on those stairs, the metal railing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there was this isolation cell. But would we see it on the photo? Where would it be? Or is it not on the photo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: It's hard here. I don't think it's shown here on the photo properly. Well, you can see the details that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which details can we see?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: The staircase leading right from the ground floor of Room 11, so they lead up, and also the railing that leads from the isolation cell, where this isolation cell was. The stairs go above the isolation cell. So everything was walled off and you could only see -- there was only the entrance. On the other side, towards the factory, there was a very small window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we do not see this isolation cell on this photo. It's somewhere else --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, no. The photograph simply doesn't show it; it's concealed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where would it be? Where would it be, left or right or ...

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: From 11, Room 11, when you come out you go right, you pass the stairway, the width of the stairway, and then you get to the door of the isolation cell where I was taken into. Perhaps it could be this that I'm pointing to now. I would have to really have a good imagination now to picture this, but I was really there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you show the -- up, up. The top photo. The witness was pointing at the right-hand side of this photo onto a wall, but we cannot see a door or something, and we do not have a better photo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, why were you taken into this solitary confinement cell?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Nobody ever told me why I was taken there. Should I mention the person who took me there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I was taken by guards who were making the lists before they knew of my identity. And before they took me to that cell they hit me and then they shut me in the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they hit you with some objects or just with the hand and how hard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. They hit me with a baton and also with their fists, and they also slapped me on my face. It was a thin guard. He was wearing gloves with the fingers cut off, on his hands. He did that under incitement by a Serb also from Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This other Serb from Foca, was he present? And how do you know that he incited the other one?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Before that, he signalled to him who I was. He knew me well. So I think that that's how it happened, that I was the first person to be taken to this solitary confinement cell in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this local Serb who indicated who you were, was he a guard or who was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, he wasn't a guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness was saying "gardisti," so knowing that the transcript is corrected later, they said "guard" as opposed to "member of the guard corps." So the Prosecutor is talking about either the guard or the member of the guard corps. So we need to know whether he was hit by a guard, a plain guard, or a member of the guard corps, whether we're talking about a regular prison guard or a member of the Serbian guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't know if we've got a very good definition of who the Serbian guards were, Mr. Bakrac. Who do you say were there in addition to the regular guards?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood the witness to talk about the voluntary guards, some kind of army, not -- not regular guards that we have been talking about in this case. I think we should differentiate between a member of the guard corps and a guard.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: May I clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: This key period from the 17th, 18th, 19th, there was chaos in the KP Dom about -- regarding the bringing and the taking away of people. There were both people assisting from Serbia. They said openly that, "We have come to help our brother Serbs," so that they switched. There were civilian police, there were members of the guards corps from Uzice, police. So any one of these would come in and they would be conducting searches, checking, looking at the things that we had with us, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I suggest that if you can, you could get the witness, as he goes, to distinguish from which particular group, if he knows, the particular guard or person he's speaking of came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. But I thought the witness had said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I thought he had too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He said he was from Serbia. He spoke about the soldier from Serbia who beat him, and there is no doubt about that. When he says "gardisti," I know that he means Serbian soldiers from Serbia, but let me clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "gardisti," do you mean the --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I mean soldiers from Serbia. Yes, exclusively that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that this soldier from Serbia hit you because a local person told him who you are, and to clarify, you said this local person was not a guard of the KP Dom but a different person. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Before the war he was a medical technician in the KP Dom. Later, he went to the front as part of the medical corps, and he didn't appear in the KP Dom any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But the point that Mr. Bakrac raises is an important one, so that when we read the transcript later on, if we have to ascribe any responsibility for these actions, we have to know whether he was a guard or whether he was somebody who came in from the outside. That's the point he is making, and it's a fair enough one. If you could just keep an eye on it so that when the witness says something about being beaten or seeing a beating, we can identify which group the person came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said already that you stayed four days in this isolation cell. Did you stay there alone?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: The third day Dr. Aziz Torlak was brought to the cell from the hospital, from work. He was also brought by a member of the guard corps from Uzice. They said, "You are going to give a statement to KP Dom," and then they left him there right up until he disappeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he disappeared. When did he disappear and how did he disappear?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I went to a different camp on July 5, 1993, and he left on July 7, 1993. He never appeared anywhere again. The Serb authorities practically admitted later that he was killed somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get out of the isolation cell? Who released you from there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Already on the 18th and the 19th, the previous guards were called back who worked in the KP Dom before and who knew how to work with convicted persons, so that there was a guard in front of my cell who I knew very well, and he also knew me. Then in four days there, I suffered from hunger and cold. There were no blankets. There was only one bed with two sheets. The same applied to my roommates, my colleagues. So we requested to be released or removed from that cell, which was later carried out. So from that cell we were taken to Room 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make a written request or did you just ask the guard, and to whom did you direct your request?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: We directed our request to the warden, and this was an oral request, and he conveyed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said "he conveyed that." Does that mean you made the request to the guard and he conveyed it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Conveyed it to whom? You said the "warden." Who was the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: The warden was Mr. Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I found that out because two guards in front of my cell, in front of the door to my cell, were having a conversation, and they said that on the 18th, Mr. Krnojelac, Milorad Krnojelac, came to be the warden and that he also had the authority, and that's how we found that out. Later, this date of when he took up this post was repeated many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this isolation cell, to which room were you taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: As I said, I was taken to Room 12. This is an area that had two Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rooms, a larger and a smaller room, and it had a kind of entrance or a hall in front of those two rooms from where you go into the toilet and also go into the two rooms, the larger and the smaller room. I was in the smaller room where there were seven or eight other detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in which building was Room 12 and on which floor?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: It was also on the ground floor, on the same level as Room 11 in building 1. I stayed in that room until August 8, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How does it come that you know the dates so well? Is there a particular reason that you remember it was the 8th of August?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: This date stuck in my memory because in the 26 months and 3 days that I spent in the camp, I went over all the events that I had lived through. I went through them over in my head, and I remember that very well. I was supposed to get an injection that day which was prescribed to me by the doctor who was taking care of the detainees, but on that day, the guard did not want to take me to the health centre so that I could receive this shot. It was a kind of cocktail. And he instead told me to get ready so that they could take me to another building and this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken from Room 12?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: From Room 12 I was taken to building 2, to Room 23. It was on the top floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in your previous statement to the investigator of the Tribunal, you mentioned that you were all the time -- for a longer period in Room 11 and not 12. Would that, then, be a mistake?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No. We're talking about Room 11. I was there for two days and two nights. Then I was in the solitary confinement cell for four days and four nights. Then I was in Room 12 until August 8th, 1992. And then I went to Room 23, then Room 18, then Room 19, then Room 15, and then again back to Room 19. I think I was transferred eight or nine times during my stay there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said Room 23 was on the top floor of the other prisoners' quarters. Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, I am sure, because you could see a fair amount of Foca. You could see the bridge over the Drina, which is quite close to the KP Dom. It was called Zeljeznicki Most, the iron bridge. You could also see the plateau of the railway station, a part of Donje Polje; you could see the bakery and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the photo Exhibit 18, photo 7528, to the witness. It's the top one.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. You can see the roof of the administration building very well, there are high trees in front of it, and you can see that this is a period of vegetation where everything is in bloom. You can see that well. You could see this -- this is what you could see from that room, number 23.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see the bridge over the Drina in front of the KP Dom, although there were these trees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. The bridge that I mentioned, the iron bridge, you could see it. I'm not sure about the other bridge which is a little bit higher, opposite the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break you mentioned to us in which rooms you were, but I would like to return with you to your stay in Room 12. When you arrived in Room 12, how many detainees were there already?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: There were already between 40 to 60 detainees there, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know these detainees from before, or some of them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, I knew a large number of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity did they have?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Most of them were Bosniaks; only one was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What age did these detainees have? Who was the youngest and who was the oldest?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Their age ranged from 17 to 65. Is it necessary to mention who the youngest person was and who the oldest person was?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. We just wanted to have the range. What about the other rooms? Could you see that there were also detainees there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. In the room that was in the other building, that belonged to the other building, because it was at the same level, there was only this small area between us and there were bars as well so we could see each other through the window and through the bars. I think it was Room 16, 16, in the other building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you estimate how many detainees were there altogether in KP Dom? Let's say in the first few months.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. I think that towards the end of May, the beginning of June, the number was the largest. It was between 600 and 650.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that? Did you count them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Quite a few of us were trying to get at the right number as to how many of us there were over there. When we would line up for lunch or for the other meal, we were counting. I did that personally as well as my colleague Dr. Torlak and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people, as far as you knew them, were they civilians or were soldiers among them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Civilians only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any sick people among you detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I would single out the group of mental patients. Two of them were in my room. I would mention a very serious mental patient, Edhem Bunda, and Hajdarevic. I'll remember his first name as well. They were both schizophrenics. And the third mental patient who was in the other building, who had had cerebral palsy in his childhood, and he walked in a bizarre fashion. He walked with his hand and arm high up like this. I would describe a patient who massacred himself. Edhem Bunda was his name. He was brought in somewhat later. He was put into that room, that porch that I mentioned. He was not in any of the rooms. His bed was in this area between the rooms. One night, he found a razor - some of us used it to shave - and he cut off part of his own ear with that razor. That took us by surprise. We had not heard anything. Of course, we reported this to the police, and he was taken to the male nurse so that this could be bandaged a bit. That was done. The next evening, again he got hold of a razor and he cut off all his fingernails on his fingers. I was taken aback by this as a physician, as were others, because we know that this is the most terrible pain that can be inflicted upon a person, tearing off fingernails. He was a mental patient, and he wandered through the forest in this area around Tjentiste, and that way he would ease his mind when he would walk through the forest. But I think that in this cooped up area, he transferred this aggression upon himself and that is why he did what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This confinement situation, did that worsen the physical stage of these mentally-ill people?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to that, it was noticeable that he was hungry. In the morning, for breakfast, when we were given hard boiled eggs, he would eat the entire egg, including the shell. Then when he would walk with us, if he could grab an insect, he would eat the insect too. We estimated that he was so hungry that he could not control his actions. In addition to him, I mentioned the man who had palsy who was in this other building. His last name was Gradisic. I can't remember his first name. He was a youngish man. And the fourth one, his name was -- I'll remember. Babic. He stayed behind me in Room 11, and out of fear he cut his veins. Later on, he was taken out in one of the groups and he was killed. He disappeared. That was a characteristic group of mental patients. Since I mentioned patients, I would like to mention another group that is noteworthy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we leave the group of mentally handicapped people, were the judges -- sorry. Were the guards aware of this particular group of people and how did they react? Did they do anything to prevent such things that you described?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. They knew who they were. They knew them. A lot of them did. But they did not take any positive action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to this group of -- this particular group of people, do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. In a later period, they were taken out of the camp together and there's been no trace of them since. I think they were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you can move on to the physically sick people.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. The other noteworthy group that we were all very upset by in the sense of what were they doing in the camp was the group of heart patients who had had heart surgery performed on them before the war. That is Asim Hadzimuratovic and Hamdija Hadzimuratovic and Rasim Jusufovic. Rasim Jusufovic and Hamdija Hadzimuratovic had double bypass operations after having a heart attack, and Asim Hadzimuratovic had had his valves replaced. And I was also surprised to see such sick people there. What did these people who were bringing such persons in think about their own future, their children, their families? That's what I thought then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The conditions -- their physical conditions, did they worsen while they were detained?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. It is only natural that after such operations such patients should undergo certain therapy, and over there they did not have the right conditions for this kind of therapy. Asim Hadzimuratovic had had an intervention and all this stopped until he got out. Later on, I think he was exchanged. I found out that he and Hamdija Hadzimuratovic died perhaps a year or two ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides you and Dr. Torlak, were there any other doctors or medical staff detained? And please, before you say the name, check if their name is on the list and then use the number, please.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. On this list there is not the name of the dentist who was brought to Livade on the next day. Oh, yes, there is. Oh, yes, there is. That is Witness 115. He was brought on the 12th of July. He was brought to Livade on the 12th of July. Then together with us, he was transferred on the 17th to KP Dom. He stayed there until I did, and he was exchanged in the same group that I was exchanged in on the 15th of June, 1994. That is Witness 115. Another witness who also belonged to the medical profession is Witness 76. He and two other witnesses were brought in directly from the hospital, from their place of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And any other doctor? Was there any other doctor?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Oh, yes. There was (redacted), Amir Berberkic. Amir Berberkic. He had been wounded, and he had also been in hospital for treatment and then was brought from the hospital to the KP Dom. He was undergoing treatment. He was supposed to have physical therapy, but all of that was interrupted when he was brought to the KP Dom. Is it necessary for me to mention the names of two other medical technicians or, rather, three of them? Later, I don't know whether Mato Ivancic, a Croat, was brought from home or from his place of work. Also, Zeco Mehmedspahic and Izet Causevic too. Those are medical technicians who were -- oh, yes. Oh, yes, yes. In Room 11 there was a young medical person who was not working yet. He had just completed medical vocational school. His name was Karabegovic; I can't remember his first name. He was taken out at an earlier stage in one group. Those were the members of the medical profession there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the detainees that were -- the other detainees that were in rooms. Were there any detainees in the isolation cells? I'm not referring to this one you were in but other isolation cells.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. In the other building, before the war there were six or seven isolation cells. Later on the prisoners built three to four solitary confinement cells in addition to that. So there were about ten of them in the other building, on the ground floor, immediately on the right-hand side. I was there one night; I spent the night in one of these solitary confinement cells. Is it necessary for me to explain right now why this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. happened?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Why were you in the isolation cell, and when?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. It was cold at the time. I think it was February or March 1993. I know it was cold. The reason was that I and Witness 215 had asked for water to bathe or, rather, to wash a bit. We asked the cook for that water and the cook allowed us; however, the policeman opposed this and asked why we didn't ask him. Since this water was being warmed outside and since the cook had approved this, we thought that that was sufficient. We walked up there, and the guard was dissatisfied with this and then he said that we should be taken to the isolation cell. And that is where we spent one night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in the isolation cell, were you mistreated or beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there, could you see or hear that there were detainees in other cells? Isolation cells, I mean.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Voices could be heard, and shouting, from both isolation cells. I can't remember the cell that we were put into. It was night-time. But on one side we could hear the conversation of two old men. I think they were caught at the Gorazde front line when food was being brought from Grebak. There was snow there and that's where they caught them. You could tell by their voices that they were elderly people. On the other side in relation to our isolation cell was a Slovenian journalist who were exercising their speaking Slovenian and who tried to battle the cold that night. That was it. Later on I know that there were other Slovenian journalists who were taken prisoner somewhere and brought in there. It wasn't only him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a particular reason why certain detainees were kept in the isolation cells and separated from the others?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Probably those who did the decision-making had their plans and had their reasons why they were putting them in there. We could not have known what this was all about. Most often these were persons who were caught at the front line. And there was no contact between us in the rooms and them. While they were in isolation cells, they had food brought to them there so that they would not establish any kind of contact with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Serb detainees or prisoners in the KP Dom while you were there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Already in 1993, I think it was May, quite a few Bosniaks had already been taken away. And when there were only 80 to 90 of us, perhaps, then they set up a prison there for their own people who had tried to escape from the front line or who had had some other mutual problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before May 1993, were there Serb prisoners in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, only at the outset, for a brief period, a night or two. These were usually Serbs from mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These Serbs, were they always kept separate? I mean the Serbs before May and after May 1993, were they kept separate from the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. But sometimes, for example, they would single out a group of us, 12, and we would stay at the same building, building 2, where there were only Serb prisoners in building 2. They were staying in several rooms. During a certain period of time we happened to be in the same building. Later on we were transferred to building 2 so that we would not have any contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let's talk about the living conditions in the KP Dom. Can you tell us how the living conditions were in winter in relation to coldness and beds available?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, there were beds, because this was an area where convicts stayed before. So we had beds, for the most part. As for the cold, there was no heating. It was very cold. I never remembered that there would be a metre and a half or even more of snow in Foca in December, as was the case that year. From the 18th of December, as far as I can remember, until the 28th, I think, the temperatures were very low. So in that period we were really freezing, especially because our food was so poor and we had so few calories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are speaking about the winter of 1992 to 1993.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: 1992. I'm sorry, 1992. As for 1993, I wasn't there when it came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This coldness, did it affect your health and the health of other detainees? And if so, in which way?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Our blood circulation was much weaker. I specifically had pains that were enhanced by the cold, but also primarily because of poor nutrition, which went on for about eight or ten months. I had a limp for a long time; my right leg was in bad shape. I had lost in that period 40 kilogrammes; that was a major loss for my organism and which was having great trouble adapting to such a weight-loss. That is one of the problems I had. In addition to that, I realised later that my eyesight was getting poorer. Also, one day when I was washing, I was simply surprised when I found edema on my legs, below my knees, which is the result of a diet that was poor in proteins. However, I was not the only person to have this kind of problem; other prisoners did as well. Some had even greater problems in this respect. I mean, those who smoked aggravated this condition because smoking does aggravate such a condition. Some also had wounds on their fingers. As for hygienic conditions which were very poor over such a long period of time, there were also lice. I did not stress until now what a major problem that was. I'm talking about human lice. But then there was also chicken lice, because they got that from the work platoon, the people who were assigned to work in the chicken coop. May I point out now that when the KP Dom was established or, rather, when the camp in the KP Dom was established, work platoons were established consisting of unskilled, uneducated persons, and craftsmen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let's talk about the work platoons later on. Let's stick with the living conditions and the results on the health of the detainees for now. You said the people got lice. How were the hygienic conditions like that this happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: The conditions were very poor. People were very close to one another. They huddled together because it was so cold and they tried to warm-up. There was no possibility to bathe so there were lice. As a physician, I was greatly surprised by this, that this kind of thing could happen. I had only read about this in books, that when hygienic conditions were very unfavourable and when people were fleeing their homes in cases of war that there could be such situations, and this was the first time I had seen this with my very own eyes. And may I just mention one more case when I had to prove to the police what was happening to all of us. One man had asked me to examine him because he said that he felt as if he were being eaten up. And I said, "I'll examine you in the morning before everybody else gets up." This man was a waiter before. And I found lots of lice on his body. In order to prove this to the police, I took a little penicillin bottle and I collected some of the lice. When the guard came to take us to breakfast, I showed him this little bottle with lice that were still alive in it. He laughed a bit and he said that he would tell the medical technician about this problem. Then later, some kind of disinfection was carried out. Something was done to get this under control. They were afraid that there would be a mass epidemic otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the bad quality of the food. Are you able to say how many calories the detainees got in that first ten months that he mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No. No, I couldn't say. But from day number one there was a prescribed dish in which meals were served. The size was prescribed. Then there was this big spoon that was used as well. In addition to that, we would get one piece of bread, one slice of bread, respectively. This was a long period of time. All the way up to May, I think, 1993. Whether they reduced the number of prisoners, then they added yet another small slice of bread, half the size of the standard slices of bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was no food available because of the war or were the rations kept deliberately so low?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I personally think that this was deliberate, because there had been lots of food at people's houses. The nutrition could have been much better, especially because in the surroundings of Foca, in Ustikolina, namely, large quantities of flour were found that they transferred to Foca, and they could have provided better food both in terms of quality and quantity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if the Serb prisoners in the KP Dom received as little food as the other detainees or was their diet different?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No. They had a better diet in all respects, in quality and quantity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I know that because if something was left over from them, sometimes we would get a part of that food. And it was tasty. It was of good quality. It was good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you lost weight. Did the other detainees also lose weight? And what about the Serb detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. A large number of Bosniak detainees also had that same weight loss. Some even lost more. I don't think the Serbs had the same weight loss because they remained for a short time and then they would leave. And they could hardly recognise some of their neighbours who had been there for a shorter or a longer time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody die due to the living conditions? I'm not speaking about beatings and torture, only the living conditions.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. The question is clear. Yes, there were a few deaths at the time that I was there and after I left. I would want to mention that Esad died. His name was Esad. I'll remember his last name. He was an electrician by trade. He had some kind of intestinal/stomach bleeding, after which he died. I think that was the first death. After that, some -- a deaf/mute person was brought from the front, from the forest. His last name was Kunovac. I can't remember his name. He also died very quickly, after some 20 days. I think he had been beaten a lot because the guards thought that he didn't want to tell them the truth, but they didn't know that he was a deaf/mute person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you are too fast. You have to pause in between and let me ask additional questions in between. You mentioned this person Esad, and on the transcript it says that you remember his last name. What was his last name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It said "I will remember." In other words, he doesn't remember now, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he die, this Esad?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. He died, I think, in May or June 1992, thereabouts. He was in another building. It's true. I was still in building 1 at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this Kunovac, when did he die and do you know the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. He died, I think, in February. It was spring 1993, to be more precise, because I know that he smelt of the forest and leaves because he had been caught in the forest, and there were a lot of leaves in his clothes from the forest. I think that he also died from some kind of internal bleeding. This was very difficult to diagnose based on some routine examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this person and did you perform this examination?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. He was right next to me, next to my bed, and that person died next to my bed. Yes. Torlak was still together with me, so the two of us together thought about what it could be. He, as a surgeon, was closer to the causes, and he probably said that it was most likely some kind of internal bleeding. He also had a kind of -- carried out a digital exam -- a manual examination of his intestine, large intestine, and he diagnosed that this person had some kind of internal bleeding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you alert the guards that something has to be done?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. We warned the guards as well as the medical technician that something was happening here. It's interesting that the guards asked that he comes with us to the place where we were eating meals, from the third floor. So he had been brought to our room. So on that day, he did manage to go, and he collapsed in the cafeteria. So when the medical technician who was in charge of that saw that, they decided that it wasn't possible for him to come to the mealtimes with the rest of us but instead they brought his food to him. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who else died?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: After I left, Ibrahim Sandal also died, yes. And then earlier, I think this was April, possibly, the beginning of May, Dzamalija committed suicide in his cell. Dzamalija. I will remember his first name. He was an older man. He was wounded during his arrest, him and his daughter. That's what we found out, that he was seriously wounded and that his daughter was seriously wounded as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to -- back to Ibrahim Sandal. When you saw him, was he sick, and what was he suffering from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I didn't get the translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ibrahim Sandal.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't hear the question, I'm sorry. Yes. He was an older man also. When I met him for the first time after I was transferred from one room to another, I found him lying down. He recognised me. He used to come to me for examinations. That's what he told me. He was exhausted. He said that he had been hiding in the woods for a long time. And when he was caught, he was beaten up, and ever since then he never really recovered. He always showed signs of sickness, symptoms of sickness. He died after I left to Kula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you alert the Judges -- sorry. Did you alert the guards in relation to the health condition of Mr. Sandal?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. They saw that because he had his food brought to him also for a while. So they would monitor whether he had really received this food to make sure that none of the other detainees ate the food. So you could see where he was lying down. He was lying down on the floor on a mattress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anyone else who died due to the conditions?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. I can't recall that anymore. There were a few cases of collapsing while we were in line waiting for our meals or while we were lined up. People would faint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any detainee who had a problem with his mouth so that he could not eat?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. One of them was Edhem Veiz. After his capture, he spent a long time in isolation. After he was released from isolation, he smelled of damp earth, and he had wounds on his lips, and he had a bad smell coming from his mouth. The other detainees complained, and they would walk away from him really. They asked me to do something about that because they couldn't stand that bad smell any more from his mouth cavity. I told the medical technician in charge, and he did give him some kind of medicine so that he could rinse out his mouth. So we did something about that so that his condition improved.
