utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But one other witness who was here before you mentioned a detainee who couldn't eat because there was something wrong with his mouth and that he died. Would you know who that was? Do you recall anything like that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know. Yes. This is another person who died. I know Kubat, Sefko Kubat, also died because of poor food and living conditions. He probably had some kind of narrowing of his intestines so that he would throw up everything he ate, and there was no way we could compensate for this by giving him IV or help him in some other way. It's true also that he died after I left for Kula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned that you were hit on one occasion. That was in the beginning. Was that the only time that you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. While I was in Foca, it was only physical abuse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see or hear other prisoners being beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. While I was in Room 12, which was not far from the administration building, then quite often I and others would hear when the physical torture started in June. We could hear loud groans and screams of people who were being physically abused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this abuse started and till when it lasted? The month, maybe.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. The abuse that I mentioned in that particular way started, according to my recollection, on June 13th, and then it went on until July 13th. It was a particular group of people. They were first taken out, the 35 people, to the administrative building. It was the rehabilitation building, because the administration building actually consisted of two parts, the administrative part and the correction department. So that's what you had, the correction department and the administrative part. So in the correction part of the building, on the ground floor, this abuse was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness again the floor plan, and this time it's 6/1. Can you put it on the ELMO so that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you put it on the ELMO so that we can see. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us the buildings that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Here is building 1 and building 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But please -- you mentioned two parts of the administration building. Can you please show us which part.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is the administration building. This is that corrections part, because the corrections department was always opposite building 1, while the administrative part was opposite building 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please put the pointer for us onto this correction part and keep it there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: This would be that part, what I'm indicating.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is pointing at the left-hand side of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the detainees get from your room or the other rooms into this building? Who took them there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: They were taken there by the police who had already taken over, as of the 17th or the 18th, all control at KP Dom. Civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "civilian police," do you mean the guards, the normal prison guards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they -- did they call out the detainees from the rooms or point them out? What was this procedure to get certain detainees into this administration building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. They would come with a piece of paper that had some names on it, names of people that they were going to take away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time of the day did they come, or did they come in the evening?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. During this period, this group would usually be taken out in the evening. They would come back to the rooms for awhile, and then after a brief period, they would take them away and then they would disappear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you heard screams. Could you see also that people were beaten, or could you only hear?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I didn't see it directly. But a number of people were taken out directly from my room, number 11, and they would come back with bruises on their faces which were a result of strong blows with items, and also they had these bruises on their legs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- at least we got the translation that you said "Room 11." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry. Room 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was taken from your room, number 12, and returned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Nurko Nisic was among the first to be taken out; then Salem Bico, called Hamdo -- Hamdo, called Salem; also Halim Konjo was taken out and his brother Halid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let us move slowly from one person to the other and discuss one person after the other. You mentioned first Nurko Nisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: According to the schedule, it is C-19, and it's also 5.27.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Nurko Nisic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Nurko Nisic was a police officer in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often was he taken out of your room, and how often was he returned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I think he was taken out once or twice, and the third time he was taken out he never came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of injuries did you see on him when he returned these one or two times?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: We saw bruises, dark bruises, on his face, also on his legs, because they were often beaten with -- they were kicked with their feet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you examine him and did you help him recover?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, we did do something, and he managed to recover. However, later he was taken out and then disappeared; he never came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he tell you, if at all? Did he tell you what happened to you and who did it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody who came back from the torture was full of fear and they spoke with fear, and some of them were so afraid that they didn't dare say anything. I think that they were threatened that if they said something they would disappear. And I think that he said that he was beaten severely all over his body and that he was beaten by Dragan Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you where he was beaten, in which room, in which part of the administration building? Do you recall anything?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. He said that that was in the corrections department, on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Hamdo Bico, also called Salem.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That is Schedule C, number 2 and also Schedule B, number 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often was he taken out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I think also he was taken out once or twice, and then later he was taken out and he did not come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see injuries on him, and what was it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Same, similar injuries as with the previous person that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you who beat him and where in the buildings?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. He said that this was on the ground floor of the mentioned building. I can't remember that he mentioned any particular person, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned Halim Konjo and Halid Konjo. That is --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. They're brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That is C-13 and B-33.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were they taken? Were they taken together? Can you explain a little bit more in detail.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, they were not taken out together. I think they were taken out once, and then the second time they were taken out they didn't come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these people? How can we distinguish between Halim and Halid?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: It's difficult. They're alike physically, I think, and also in their behaviour. They had a cafe in Foca. They're father had the cafe, and that's where they worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see injuries on them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. They also had physical injuries on their skin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if both of them disappeared?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was taken from your room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Brothers Rikalo were taken out from Room 12. These are three brothers. They were taken out individually, in different periods. It is to be noted about them that they escaped from Foca, they were caught in Montenegro, and then they were brought to the Foca camp. Also, there were other deportations like that of small groups of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the first names of the three brothers?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Zaim Rikalo, Hido Rikalo, and I can't recall right now the third one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hido, is that a nickname? Could that be --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, no. It's a name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Rikalo brothers are C-21 to C-23, and also incidents B-45 to B-48.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these Rikalo brothers taken on several occasions, and did you see them return injured?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No. I think they were called out once, in the evening. They were taken out and they disappeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyone else from your room, Room 12?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I can't remember right now whether any more people were taken out in this period that we're talking about, from the 13th of June. But I know that a number -- a large number of people were also taken out from Room 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall who was taken out from Room 11, or any other room, whom you saw?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. The medical technician, Karabegovic, was taken out; I can't remember his name now. Adil Granov was taken out; he was an engineer. Also Krunoslav Marinovic, a Croat, was taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let's, again, go one by one so that we do not have to repeat them.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Karabegovic return with injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I can't describe the injuries in detail. I know he was wearing a kind of green fur coat. He passed by our window. Our window looked directly out onto the yard and the path that you would go to and come back from building 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often was Mr. Karabegovic taken out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I think once or twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already mentioned Adil Granov. How often was he taken out?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: By the way, this is C-9 and B-22.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. About the same. He was taken once or twice to interrogations and to be tortured, and after that he disappeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed to the next person you remember.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: The next person was Zulfo Veiz. And Veiz -- I remember Zulfo was a police officer and Veiz -- this is the son of this person that I described earlier, Edhem, who was in the isolation cell. Veiz, I'm not quite sure whether he was in Room 11. Maybe he was in Room 15 directly above for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often was Mr. Zulfo Veiz taken out and did you see him return with injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. He was taken out once or twice in the same way and after that he disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is the person C-29, and incident 5.27 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You have missed one out. The witness had earlier referred to a Croatian by the name of Krunoslav Marinovic, and you may not want him, I don't know, but he had mentioned him before you said, "Let's take them one by one."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. I missed -- but I have him here on my list but I missed him. When -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move now to Mr. Marinovic. That's C-17 and also incident 5.27. What can you tell us about him? How often was he taken and did you see him return?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned him already, that he was taken while I was still at Livade, on the second or the third day which was at Livade. He was brought from his wife's summer home, weekend house. His wife's name is Slavica. He was beaten. He had a fractured jaw. He was beaten. He was in a lot of pain. Then he was in Room 11. He was also taken out once or twice in this period. After that, he disappeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you have -- who else? You have mentioned Zulfo Veiz. Is there another Veiz?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The name Veiz, he was a merchant. Munib is his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the person C-28 and B-59 [Realtime transcript read in error "C-58 and B-29"]. What can you tell us about Munib Veiz? How often was he taken out and did you see him return?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. He was taken out two or three times or perhaps even more. I think they must have had a reason concerning him. Later on, he was taken in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him being injured, return injured from the beatings?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, I could not explain any injuries in detail because the path is about 1 metre, 2 metres in front of the windows, but he looked in a very sorry state as he was being returned, and he seemed concerned too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Munib Veiz a relative of Zulfo and Edhem?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: He's Edhem's son and he is Zulfo's relative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anyone else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned in that group of four mental patients this young man who had cut his veins, Babic. I can't remember his first name. He was also taken out in this group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Asim Mezbur?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Asim Mezbur, yes, a photographer. He had an arm missing, probably since birth. He was taken out in that group. Later on, I think his brother Esad was also taken out. It is correct that he was taken out, but I think that the brother was taken out later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, Asim Mezbur is B-41.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a certain Hajro Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, Sabanovic. There were two of them, actually. What is characteristic of them, notably one of them whose behaviour was sometimes Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. slightly abnormal, and this particularly came to the fore in the prison. He had a nickname, and for a long time he was in the same cell where I was locked up. And he was beaten up very severely there because he quarreled with the police. He was dark, tall. There was another Sabanovic too who was a worker at the Maglic company.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, Hajro Sabanovic, that is B-41 [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was you or the court reporters, but the earlier reference to Munib Veiz, according to the transcript, was "C-58 and B-29." It should be B-28 and C-59.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm quite sure I said it the right way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, as long as we get it right somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It is very helpful that we have these references so that we can check the transcript against the particular incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And I didn't check the transcript, so I didn't see that mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But I can see it would be a very easy mistake for anybody to have made, wherever it occurred, as long as we get it right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Hajro Sabanovic, was he also in this group of people taken between the 13th of June and the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I cannot recall whether he was taken out in that group. He was taken out though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said he quarreled with a guard and, as a result, he was beaten. With which guard did he quarrel and do you know who beat him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I cannot recall. It depended on the shift concerned, which guard was on duty. They worked in shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Avdo Mehmedspahic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I know that name very well. He was taken prisoner somewhat later. After having spent eight days in an isolation cell, he was brought precisely to my room. I think this was the month of July. He had evident injuries that he had sustained while he was being taken prisoner or, rather, in this corrections building he described a room to us there that is a torture chamber, a chamber for torturing people. He described some kind of chains and belts that are used to tie up people's limbs so that a person cannot defend himself while being beaten. And he had a very evident wound in his knee, edema with water and blood in the knee. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is the incident B-40.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when this happened to him, that he was beaten in this part of the prison?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: He was being beaten up as he was brought in, before he was to be locked up in the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall a Mandzo, Salko Mandzo? Do you recall this person?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. There were two Salko Mandzos there. One was a more corpulent one. He was a manual worker in the public utilities company. He had a nickname too. When torture was to be carried out, he was mistaken for another Salko Mandzo who was very small and of slight build. He was physically injured with something that he described as a knife. Also, his earlobe was injured and the skin on his neck. When they injured him in that way, he spent that first night after that in an isolation cell, and it was only on the next day that he was brought to our room. So that was while I was still in Room 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is the incident 5.28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you've given us the description of B-41 to two different witnesses now, and when you look at the Schedule B, 41 appears to be only one person and is given the letters "MA". You've given us Hajro Sabanovic and Asim Mezbur for B-41.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think the Asim Mezbur B-41 should be the right one. Obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It looks like it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just -- it's -- it's Mr. Hajro Sabanovic that is 49, B-49.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mandzo tell you what happened to him and where he was injured?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. He is the one who told us about all of this. That is how we found out that all of this happened in this corrections building, as it was always called, on this ground floor, in this room where these tortures and abuses were carried out. Somebody recognised him and said that that's not the one that was important for them, and that is how he, fortunately, managed to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he tell you who recognised him and recognised the mistake?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, I think he said, but I can't remember right now. I can't remember the name of this person and these persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this other Mandzo, the lighter one, was he taken then instead? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. He never showed up again. He is from this Muslim neighbourhood, so to speak, of Donje Polje. Whoever was from Donje Polje could hardly survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned these beatings between the 13th June to the 30th June. How long did these beatings generally last in the evenings? When did they start and when did they end?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: They would start sometime around dusk. Well, it depended. Sometimes it would even be while there was still daylight. It was summertime, when night falls late, and then it would go on deep into the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything else except for the screams and the beatings? Did you hear anything else on such evenings?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. We would hear the shouting of these persons who were doing this. Then sometimes people from my room would hear the sound of something falling into the water. Then also there would be shooting in front of the administration building and also one could hear noise coming from vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me clarify something. You said that people from your room would hear the sound of falling -- that something was falling into the water; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No. I said that it was closer to people who were above my room. I mean, I was on the ground floor, so it was more difficult to hear something like that. So we were told about this when we went to lunch or breakfast or some other meal if we were allowed contacts. Then we would also see injuries on these persons that I described as being taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the Schedule C, that is the Exhibit P55.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we have already mentioned several of the people from this list, and, therefore, we do not have to discuss all of them. I will now refer you from one to the other, and you are requested to tell us what you know about these people. The first person, number 1, Alija Altoka, do you know this person, and what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. He was taken out of the camp. I don't know the exact date. Also, we already talked about person number 2 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please wait for my question. It's easier when we do it in a more organised way. Was this person taken out in the month of June, as you have already described, or was he taken out at a different time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I could not state exactly whether he was taken out in this first group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Please move on to person number 3, Abdurahman Cankusic. What do you know about him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: He also disappeared. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that he disappeared, and also Mr. Altoka disappeared, did they disappear in connection with beatings or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, they were taken out, and until the present day there's been no trace of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you hear the sound of beating when these -- when Mr. Altoka or Mr. Cankusic were taken out? Was it the same -- similar to what you have described before or different?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Bakrac please turn on his microphone. We can't hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. I think that the witness was clear enough when he answered the question, when he said they were taken out of the KP Dom and that there's been no trace of them since. I think that this is a leading question in relation to something that is being contested. Beforehand, he already talked persons about which he had heard had been beaten, and if I understood things correctly, we are going to skip over these persons' names on this list now. So I think this was a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think that's so, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. You can ask the witness whether -- I think you actually asked him whether any other incident occurred at the time they were last seen. But to lead him directly into were there any beatings, I think, may be a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In fact, I'm sure of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It was my understanding that I had asked him before who returned. Up till now we have only spoken about those who he saw return and who were taken afterwards, and now I wanted to actually discuss with him only to find out if these people also belonged to groups of beaten people or if they were taken away otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's so. But have you got any material from this witness yet as to whether number 3 had been beaten? I don't think you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, your question was: "... did they disappear in connection with beatings or otherwise?" Now, adding the words "or otherwise" doesn't stop it from being a leading question. As I suggested, I think you'd asked him sometime early, you should ask: Was there any other incident which happened at the time that they were last seen or taken out for the last time?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you heard what the Presiding Judge had mentioned. Was there any incident when Mr. Cankusic was taken away?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to number 4, Refik Cankusic, what can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. He was taken out once or twice. Later he went missing. He has a brother, Abdurahman; we'll see whether his name is here. These are two brothers who disappeared. Also, their father, Hasan, was taken prisoner as well. He's still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Refik was taken twice -- you said once or twice. Did you see him return on one occasion?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Once he was taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was only taken out once?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any incident on the day he was taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next person, number 5, Enko Cedic.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I think that the first name is not correct here. The last name is all right. If this is a person with a degree in law from Tjentiste, then that's him. He also disappeared. I can't remember when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what would be the correct name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I knew him personally - he's a young man - but I really cannot remember whether this is his real name or whether he had a different name. But the last name is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned the person at number 6, Juso Dzamalija. Do you know why he committed suicide?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, I think because of the severe wounding and the family tragedy he experienced. Also, the police were saying that he had a son in Sarajevo and they held it against him, so that was an aggravating circumstance in his case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "they held it against him," was he beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: That I don't know. I did not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving to the person at number 7, Kemal Dzelilovic, what can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. This is a young man. I think he had a degree in engineering. He was taken prisoner. He was also taken away in that group of 35 men that we keep mentioning. His father was with me in Room 12, Halim. Halim or Halil, I can't remember exactly. He was sad when he found out that his son had been taken out and had disappeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person at number 8, Ramo Dzendusic.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: He was taken prisoner somewhere up there near Montenegro, in his village. I don't know whether he survived, whether he's still alive or whether he's missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now the person at number 10, Nail Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. He is a person who was also in this group of 35 missing persons. He's an elderly man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 11, Mate Ivancic.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, this is also a medical technician by profession. He worked in the hospital. He's a Croat, an ethnic Croat. I don't know exactly when he was taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person, Esad Kiselica, number 12.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, that's the person we mentioned a few minutes ago, the one I could not remember, who died at an early stage because of that bleeding. Think back. Can you remember that, when we mentioned that a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that the last name is Kiselica? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know an Esad Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know Esad Hadzic too. Right, yes. Esad Hadzic and Esad Kiselica, I always kept taking one for the other. I knew who they were, but I think that now again I've taken one for the other. I think that Hadzic was the one that we discussed a few minutes ago. I don't know what happened to Kiselica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now number 14, Adil Krajcin.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is noteworthy. I knew him well. He's also a young man. He worked in the mine as an economist. He was taken prisoner due to an unfortunate incident when he went to see his apartment in Foca. He was taken out precisely on the 1st or 2nd of August, 1992 with two brothers, I think. Their names are -- oh, I'll remember their names. But they are from Miljevina. I can't see their names here. They're called Dzanko. These two brothers, they're young men, they were taken together with him, with this man named Krajcin. They're not here on this list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any incident on that day, on the 1st or 2nd of August?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was fighting at the Trnovo front line, there were persons killed there, and the police very quickly, in broad daylight, ran into the compound, searched for him and these two that I mentioned, the Dzanko brothers, and the three of them and yet another person, I think, were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. We'll resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, we had already discussed number 14. Let's move to number 15 of Schedule C, Mustafa Kuloglija. What can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Could I have the list, please. The person under number 15, Mustafa Kuloglija, was also captured. He was also in the camp. He disappeared, I think, in this group that we mentioned, this group of 35. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next one, Fuad Mandzo, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I think he was also a medical technician. So that I add on to what I said earlier regarding the number of medical staff who had been captured. As far as I can recall, one of the Mandzos was also captured and he was a medical technician. I think this is him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know how he disappeared? Was he in the group of 35 or did he disappear differently?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I can't say how he disappeared. He just disappeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next person, number 17. We have discussed number 18. Number 18, Omer Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I think there is a mistake in the name here. The last name is correct, Mujezinovic. Samir. Samir Mujezinovic. He was wounded at Ustikolina. He was brought to the hospital for treatment where he spent a certain amount of time, after which he was brought to the camp. I will tell you the exact date that he was taken out in another group. This is a young man, a young person, a student of technical sciences. So he was brought to the camp from the hospital as a sick person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when -- and how did he leave the KP Dom; when?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: He left KP Dom on September 17, 1992, in a large group of 45 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a particular reason why he was taken out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, this was a large group of people who were taken out, so I couldn't really say why he was taken out as well if the others were taken out at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next person, number 20, Hamid Ramovic.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Hamid Ramovic, yes. I know this person well. He had come to bury his brother Abid Ramovic, who was killed on April 8th close to the railway station. He was shot by a Serb sniper in his car, through his heart, and he was killed instantly, his brother. So in three or four days, he came to bury him. Then on the way back, he was captured at Livade and brought to the camp KP Dom. Then he disappeared in one of the groups. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next three persons, you already mentioned the brothers Rikalo but you could not remember their first names, at least of some of them. If you look --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Here is the third one. We mentioned Husein Rikalo, Zaim Rikalo, and their third brother is Mithat Rikalo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. But you also mentioned a Hido, Hido Rikalo. He is not here on this list.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Then we have the question whether Hido was maybe a nickname from Husein. Husein, Hido. I think that's it. And then Husein is his real name, his Bosnian name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the person number 24, Seval Soro.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know him. He was also arrested, and he spent some time with us in the camp and then he also disappeared in one larger group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person Kemal Tulek, number 25.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. The same as Soro and the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 26, Enes Uzunovic.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. The thing that is characteristic for him is that he was tortured for a long time. He had been beaten a lot. He's also a medical technician. So I add on to my earlier statement about the number of medical technicians. He was working at the medical centre, i.e., the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said he was tortured and mistreated several times. Did you see him return and did you see injuries on him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. He had bruises on his face, on his body. I did see him, and I think that he had spent some time in the isolation cell where I was also kept the first time. Yes, I could see him at the door. I don't know when he was taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 27, Vahida, Dzemal Vahida.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. He was taken out at the same time as the above-mentioned Mujezinovic, on the 17th of September, 1992. He was a police officer, and he was arrested or captured at his home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he taken out of room -- of his room on several occasions or only this one time when you said that he disappeared?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Only once. I remember the time that he disappeared, on the 17th of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The other people on the list we have already discussed. Did you ever hear --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of any of these people from this list? Did they -- had anybody ever seen them again or did their bodies turn up?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This pattern of beatings and the disappearances, how did this affect you personally and also the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Of course this created a lot of fear amongst each one because we would be asking ourselves, "When am I going to be next?" And of course we would feel panic in the evening when the armed guards would appear and start taking people out. This is a terrible fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you figure out a reason why these particular detainees we have discussed were taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No. But you could conclude that these are generally young people, and then specially, in certain cases of the -- with certain exceptions such as the Dzamalija. But otherwise these are all young people, healthy, and I could really say that they had gone to be liquidated, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or other detainees ever complain about this to the guards or to anyone else of the prison staff?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, we did complain to the guards about what was happening to the people, starting from this group of people in June that we talked about, but there was no reaction in any positive sense. They would just shrug their shoulders. "We don't know anything. Others make decisions about that."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they said "others," did they indicate whom they would mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Probably the number one person, the warden of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interrogated while you were in the prison?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. On two occasions I was taken to the administrative building for interrogation, to that left part, the central administration building. I think this was probably somewhere on the second floor. Perhaps the first floor. I can't remember precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Both times I was interrogated by Zoran Vladicic, who worked as an inspector before. Also, besides him, in other rooms, interrogations were carried out by Koprivica - I can't remember the name - and I will remember the name of the third person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you to the administration building for the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I couldn't hear the witness' answer.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I was taken by the police to the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean the guards in the prison when you said --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you asked? What was the interrogation focused on?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: They knew me quite well, my movements, and they just wanted to be convinced one more time about what they already knew very well, what my movements were before the attack on Foca, my activities, whether I had any particular actions related to the party. So that was it. The second time they called me to explain two photographs which were found in my apartment - they were not clear to them - from my family album.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you accused of anything in particular? Were you informed about any charges?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No. The interrogator never told me that, nor did anybody else. There were occasions when there were provocative questions, when there was a group of journalists who came. The Crisis Staff had prepared a set of questions, and then one of the provocative questions asked then was, "Why did the party support the line of Islamisation of Serbs?" and what I thought about that. There was another question which was quite insulting to me which was asked by a young lady journalist who said that she worked for a press agency from Novi Sad, but she was actually from Foca. I knew her very well. Her name was Vesna. I asked her, "Aren't you ashamed to ask me such a question? This is a provocative question and it's aimed against me and my character. In the given situation, it's a very deliberate question," and she just remained silent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this take place?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I think this happened between the 1st and the 4th of May in 1992. I was still in Room 12 at that time. But besides this provocative question, there was another question also about what I thought about the return of Muslims to Foca, in view of the fact that the town had been quite destroyed. So this was a question for me. I answered: "Really, I don't know since I have no idea anymore of what the town looks like, because I have been in detention for 20 or more days."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This discussion with the group of journalists, where did it take place? Was it in the open or also in one of these interrogation rooms?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No. This happened in Room 12, in the presence of the police there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to this meeting with the journalists, you said the Crisis Staff had organised questions. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Everything indicated that, everything pointed to that, so it was my conclusion that really such questions could only come from the Crisis Staff; from the Crisis Staff of the SDS, of course, which at that time managed or conducted all the operations, until the civilian and the military structures were separated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you prepared -- did you know that the journalists were coming, and did someone prepare you for this visit?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed before to get ready, to get dressed, to put my suit on, to come out into this little hall in front of the two rooms, and that's where this conversation took place. I was there and a number of other detainees were present, including Gordan Hukovic, who also disappeared in the group that disappeared on the 17th of September, 1992. He was a Croat. He was the third Croat out of the four Croat detainees to disappear. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell the journalist about the abuse and the bad conditions?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, no. They didn't even ask me that. This Hukovic, he could speak French, and he said that he told them that we were being treated like cattle here, that we're hungry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us return to the interrogation. You said that you were interrogated twice. Were you mistreated during your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, they didn't abuse me personally, but I could hear in the nearby rooms that they were mistreating people during interrogation. I knew a young man who was 20 years old, Adnan Berberkic. He was abused quite a lot and he was beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When? When was that, during your first or your second interview?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: This was during the second interrogation, which I think took place sometime in early June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see detainees being beaten in the yard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No. No. They did that undercover.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see detainees being beaten on their way to the canteen or even in the canteen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. There were police officers who would strike somebody. They would strike one of the prisoners lightly or more heavily while you were going through the door. Amongst them, the guard Milenko Burilo was mentioned because he had the habit of doing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see soldiers from outside mistreating and beating detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. I think this happened only once when one of the rooms -- the people in the rooms were aligned to go for lunch and soldiers appeared. They went inside and then they hit a few people who were waiting in line to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when that happened, in which room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. I was in building 2. I think I was in Room 23 or 18. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were detainees exchanged, and, if so, when did it start?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: All of these groups that I mentioned as having been taken out, the guards told us that they were going to be exchanged. So all of these things happened under the pretext that they were going to be exchanged. However, later we found out that these were not exchanges. We found that out from the guards and also from Serbs who later came to the camp - I think this was perhaps later in December - that these were not exchanges. So the largest number of people disappeared in this way and only a small number of older people were exchanged in the Trnovo front at the end of 1993 -- 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that guards later confirmed that these detainees disappeared. When -- what did the guards say about these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: They always would say, "They went to be exchanged and we don't know any more about this." But then we would ask, "So how come none of them are getting in touch with us after several months or more?" But they would avoid any conversation about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your estimation of how many detainees disappeared in these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Under such, quote/unquote, "exchanges," about 400 people disappeared, but in the camp, the people who survived numbered 200.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, as a medical person, did you have conversations with the medical staff in the KP Dom about the fate of detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Not particularly, but there were questions to the medical technician and also to the doctor who was engaged, who was there to come and examine the detainees. He disappeared in December 1992, and we found out that he had fled Foca with his family, that he had fled to Serbia. He told me at the health centre personally that there is great danger for all of us who are in the camp, and I asked him why. And he said, "Depending on which Serb gets killed on the front, three to five people -- three to five of you would disappear here." And, yes, this is what really happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did he tell you that and who is he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: This happened in early May, when Foca was already captured completely and when they were going towards Gorazde. His name was Cedomir Dragovic. He was a doctor. The second person who was also in charge of health of the detainees, and he was there until I was there, was Gojko Jovanovic. He was an older person. He was retired before the war. In the period of aggression, they employed him to do these tasks even though he was retired. He made a list of people so that they could each say what illnesses they suffered from under the pretext that these sick people would be sent for exchange. This happened in September 1992. Of course, we were happy, and we told him what we suffered from. We told him about our illnesses, but, however, the opposite actually happened. The sick people remained behind and the people who were healthy left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to work in the prison?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, I didn't have to work in this camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever registered by the ICRC while in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No. The first time the Red Cross came to the KP Dom, on the 23rd of June, 1992, and a group of 12 people, including me, were taken in the early morning hours in a police vehicle to the basement of the bakery, which was quite close to the KP Dom, and that is how they did not enable us to be registered by the Red Cross. But other detainees who remained behind who were registered said where we were, because a large number of us -- they had said that a large number of us or a group of us had been hidden. They managed to say that so that our certificates from the International Red Cross state a date which was confusing to us. So it wasn't the date when we were actually arrested, but it was the date when the International Red Cross found out that is where we were or our relatives looked for us. So ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to actually do work in the bakery or were you hidden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. It was true that they said that we would have some lighter tasks and that we would get bread, and it's true that this was a contrived situation in order that they could remove us from there. So it wasn't really any kind of important or significant work that we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything particular about you and the other 11 or 12 people who were taken to the bakery?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: They waited until it was dark and then they returned us to the camp, inside the camp, without giving us any explanation. It was one specific thing that the guard made a mistake and he took us down the street before it got dark. So they attacked him for taking us along the street, on the street. So this was taken as a sort of failing of his.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question was: Was anything particular about you? What kind of people were you, the 12 of you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, in that sense. Yes. It was a group comprising mostly intellectuals. So we remained as a separate group throughout that time, before the arrival of the Red Cross and then after that. So we did remain as a separate group that was not registered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden of the KP Dom while you were detained there. Do you know what happened -- what became of the prewar warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: He withdrew from that space upstairs or to where the women's prison was. So he was kind of dislocated. He was out of the town of Foca where the Crisis Staff was. That's where the warden was before. Shortly before the war, the colleague who actually worked in KP Dom as a regular employee, I know that he would phone me or he called me at the health centre and he asked me whether we had any medicines that the warden needed, and I said, "Where is the warden?" And he said, "He's at Brioni," and this is the place where the women's prison is situated. So that's where he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, that reference to where he phoned him, is that an identifiable feature?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It also includes the hospital. People refer to the hospital as well as the health centre. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So it's all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this former warden -- did you see him in the KP Dom during your confinement there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, I never saw him. We knew one another well personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, the then warden, did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, we knew each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know him? How good?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Due to the nature of my work and due to the nature of his work, in a way, that led to our contacts at a professional and human level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of professional contacts did you have with Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: He worked in school, (redacted) (redacted), so that was this professional contact that we had. Later there were also some contacts, (redacted) (redacted). Sorry. May I just add something to this. Mr. Krnojelac worked in a school; he was a teacher. He was (redacted)teacher for about a year or a year and a half. He taught her math.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Mr. Krnojelac come to you (redacted)? How long before the war was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, that was just before the war. I think it was March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he behave usual -- in the usual way, or did you notice something?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, he seemed angry to me, anxious, as if the entire situation that was evolving in town and around it had affected him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything, how he was affected and why he was anxious?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: No, no. This is just what I inferred (redacted) by his behaviour. We did not particularly discuss the situation, especially not politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the family of the accused?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. For awhile I knew his sons and his wife. Later on they grew up and I wasn't always sure of who they were. I couldn't always recognise them; they're quite similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was one of the sons of Mr. Krnojelac wounded during the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We found out -- we heard that he had been wounded, but of course I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall when the son was wounded and how?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I think that was June/July 1992, one of those two months, as far as I can remember. He stepped onto a minefield.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this event reflect in any way the treatment in the KP Dom? Did it change after this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, yes. Guards were strict, angry. Also the kitchen staff. That made us even more fearful. It had a negative impact on our overall condition. Also in terms of food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean, "in terms of food"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, the bare minimum was given, what they had to give, so to speak, in that period, during this critical period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you knew Mr. Krnojelac from before the war, was he a member of any party; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I personally think he was a member of the SDS; otherwise, he would not have been appointed to that position. That position could only be enjoyed by someone who was greatly trusted by the SDS, because there was no other Serb party in Foca except for the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were detained, did you ever talk personally with the accused?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we had two contacts. The first contact was late in April, when I got out of the cell that I mentioned. I asked for a contact with my family so that they would know that I was alive. People only knew that I was taken in an unknown direction. So this was made possible for me. I was given the possibility of establishing telephone contact with my wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To have this conversation with your wife, who -- what did you actually do? Did you write to the warden or did you just request to see him? Can you explain it in more details, please.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I sent a request through the guard. Since I knew him and he knew me, as I explained to you, there was this human respect, to put it that way, like before the war when there were good relations between Serbs and Muslims. He accepted. The guard came to get me from the room and I was brought to his office, and I made a telephone call to my wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His office, where was it in the buildings?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The usher is gone, but my colleague can put Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Exhibit 6/1 onto the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point out where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, the first time I was taken from Room 12. Along these short steps and the short path to this administrative building, there was this heavy metal door there which had a very characteristic sound that we prisoners will never forget. Every time you would hear that door bang you would know that somebody was either being brought in or taken out. And then you take this short hallway to the left, and there was some kind of a room for visitors to previous convicts. That was on the ground floor. This belonged to the central administration building rather than to the building of corrections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you were moving around with this pointer. Can you put your pointer on the room that you just mentioned as the visitors' room.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: See here? This is the canteen, the former canteen. Wait a minute. Or next to the canteen. This is the room for visitors here. Ground floor. What does it say over here? What does it say here? Yes. Okay. That's it. I think it was here. I think it was here. Here, it's marked 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: And this hall where it says "Sala," that's where it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness just said it's the Sala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's been saved. Unfortunately, of course, we have the problem that at the time when the witness is using the pointer, he is saying something which we don't get the translation for for some few seconds. But I think it's saved now. He was, indeed, intending to point to the Sala and the rooms marked 1 and 2, and that can be noted in the transcript. It doesn't matter where he's pointing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came to this room Sala, was Mr. Krnojelac already in the room? And if so, was he alone?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, he was there, and I think his son. He was in camouflage uniform, both he and his son. His son was armed. There was a regular exchange of greetings, and conversation was brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Usher, you can leave this position now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the son was armed. What kind of arms did the son have?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: As far as I know and as far as I can remember now, it was a Kalashnikov or something. I am not very knowledgable about weapons. I know the old rifle of the former JNA that I had when I did my military service, that M-82, because I had exercises with that weapon when I did my regular military service. And never again was I interested in weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said they had camouflage uniforms. Do you mean a military camouflage uniform or police?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Military camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Krnojelac have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I did not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the son's function? Why was he there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, he was like a bodyguard, like security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said the conversation was very brief. What was said?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I managed to reach my wife to tell her that I was near Foca. I did not dare say the place; I was not supposed to say where I was exactly. I said I was well. I said that she should take care of the children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what did you speak with Mr. Krnojelac about? What did he say? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, after saying hello to one another, we practically complained about the situation to one another by mimic. And he said, "Well, Doctor, there is a war going on. There is a catastrophe." He was justifying everything by this war situation. He mentioned that his house had burned down -- that his house burned down as well, and that all of this was a misfortune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak about the conditions at the KP Dom and why you were there? Did you ask him or did he say anything -- did he himself say something?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I did not ask him why I was there. I mean, there were a lot of people already in the camp. Well, "camp" is not a word that was permitted. It was prison. So we kept using the word "prison" rather than "camp." And also I was saying that it would be a good thing to have medical care as soon as possible; that's what we talked about. And we said that Cedomir Dragovic, a colleague who worked with convicts in the prison before that, would be a good idea, a person who was familiar with the method of work, just as I did this too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this conversation, did you try to see Mr. Krnojelac again?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was this critical period of June/July. I sent requests in writing and orally, asking him to receive me, because I realised that I was still losing weight and I was wondering whether something could be done about an exchange and an overall improvement of conditions in the camp, especially because some kind of exchange of prisoners from Foca for prisoners from Sarajevo was being mentioned, and that had greatly pleased us. And we were living in the hope that this would happen as soon as possible, so I wanted to talk to him about that, in that sense. However, I could not reach him; he would not receive me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said you saw him twice. When was the second time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: When I say twice, I mean this direct contact. I saw him many times moving about with the guards through the compound, around the compound, as he was carrying out his duties as a warden, from my room, from various rooms where I was standing. And on the 10th of June, 1993, we had our other, second, direct contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you request this contact, this second direct contact?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and this was in writing. And this was made possible for me; namely, we talked once again in the same room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was present besides you and Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, at that time I can't remember, really, whether there was anyone else who was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Krnojelac wearing that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I can't remember now. I think it was still a uniform, a military uniform. We were already used to seeing it, to seeing people in that uniform, people who had these duties. As for the conversation, my questions were what would happen to us, that I was ill. Already then I could not walk downstairs from the third floor to the canteen. My leg hurt me a lot. So I asked for food to be brought to me, to my room, because I could not manage to walk downstairs so fast and get out like the rest of them. And the guards were telling me to hurry up, so I couldn't even manage to eat what I was given. In that period, I had my ration of food brought to me in the room. And I was seriously concerned about my condition. That was the main reason why I requested another meeting with him as he was the person responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you when you spoke about your condition?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: He said that it did not depend upon him, really; that he could not influence my exchange because it was a higher command that was deciding on that, that's what he told me, his Superior Command. Then he mentioned something to me that greatly surprised me and worried me, when he said that a few days before that he had attended a meeting in Bijeljina with all wardens of camps from all over Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that general camp problems were discussed at that meeting. And he said, unfortunately it was not only that camp, but that practically every municipality had a camp. I was astonished by this revelation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Bijeljina? You mentioned he went to Bijeljina for a meeting.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Bijeljina is to the north-east. It is a big municipality on the north-east -- in the north-east of Bosnia. It is flat land, and it borders on Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he indicate how many camps? You said you got the impression that every municipality had a camp. What did he say exactly that you got this impression?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: That is precisely what he said: "Unfortunately, it is not only this camp. All municipalities have camps." And I was assured of that. I realised that, indeed, things were so when I came to Kula. Soon after that I went to Kula, and in Kula I met people from Grapska, Doboj, Banja Luka, Visegrad, many places, Zvornik, Bijeljina, Batkovic, the camp of Batkovic. That's where I met camp inmates from many municipalities. From Rogatici as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak about the bad living conditions with him on that occasion, especially the food situation?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: We mentioned that problem too, but what was said was that nothing could be done about that. There was a war that was well under way. What was said was that nothing special could be done in respect of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he mentioned his Superior Command. Did he indicate who that was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, indirectly, it was logical that it was some kind of a military command to which he was subordinated. And he said that they were there as a service of this military command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet or hear who the military commander was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. A group of prisoners, three of them all with the last name of Cengic, went early one morning to be interviewed by him and Milan Kovac, the commander of the units in Foca. They were supposed to go to Belgrade and be freed somehow in that way. However, that would not happen on that day. When they talked to them in the morning hours and when the guards told them that they would be going that day, because there was a problem of gasoline or whatever in terms of reaching Belgrade. So this group returned to our room and told us that the commander had lectured them, that it was impossible to live with Muslims anymore, and that it was high time for the Serbs to live and that there will be no more life with you. So people -- these people returned to the room quite frightened. Is it necessary for me to mention names?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to hear from you first. You have mentioned Cengic. When? When was that? Which month or even day? When did this conversation take place?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I think this was January/February 1993. It's 1993 mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Cengic, who were they, those three you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: That's a group of related persons who lived in a small place, Miljevina. One of them was blind; his name was Fehim. The other one was quite old; his name was Nezir. He was about 80 years old when he was brought to the camp. He had been treated in hospital before that. So he was brought from hospital directly to the camp. He had had a heart attack. The third one was somewhat younger. His name was Hilmo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these three persons, did they tell you -- did they mention who was present besides this military commander Kovac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. They mentioned Mr. Krnojelac and Mr. Kovac, that they were there, that they conducted this interview with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you spoke twice to Mr. Krnojelac. Do you know if any other detainees spoke with Mr. Krnojelac --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- personally and would you know what they talked about?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: I think there were other people who talked to Mr. Krnojelac, among them Professor Husein Lojo and his brother Dzevad, and I think a few other people during that long period of time had brief contacts. I cannot recall right now what they said to us, what kind of a conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And besides Mr. Krnojelac, who was the second in command? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: The second in command was his deputy, Savo, Savo Todovic. Todovic, Savo Todovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a special function within the prison? Did he have special tasks?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Well, that was the second person in command in the camp hierarchy, the first one after Mr. Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the prison and did you ever talk to him personally?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we talked twice, I think, with regard to the same issues that we already mentioned: bad living conditions, bad hygienic conditions, poor food, things like that. That is to say that I talked to him about twice, briefly. The answer was that nothing could be done, that that's the way things were. Other people also had such brief contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall who was the commander of the guards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Nikola Rasevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to him personally about the living conditions?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Not particularly, in view of the fact that his position was different, although our problems were often mentioned to the guards as well. When people are in trouble, they talk about it to everyone. Everyone seeks help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw Mr. Todovic and Mr. Rasevic in the prison, what did they wear?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Sometimes they were in uniform and sometimes they were in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "uniform," do you mean a military uniform or a police?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Military uniform and also civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards in the prison, what did they wear?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: They wore the usual guard's uniform which they had before the war, but often they also had a military uniform so that they would wear different uniforms, if I may say so, camouflage uniforms, the multicolored ones, standard police uniforms, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned one guard who hit detainees. You said Burilo, Burilo did that. Do you recall any other --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111
utterances.text: Milenko Burilo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
